candidate.scope: The assigned middle Illumina row, labelled sci-RNA-Seq (Single-cell combinatorial indexed RNA sequencing), interpreted at schematic scope as the two-round RT/PCR indexing implementation described by Cao et al. (2017). sci-RNA-Seq and sci-RNA-seq are spelling/capitalization aliases here. Cells and nuclei are alternative compartment inputs named by this row. The cropped SPLiT-Seq row above, CEL-Seq row below, and chemical structure at the right are neighboring catalogue material, not target alternatives or connected assay branches. Three illustrated wells in each round retain separate local operations under shared captions; they do not specify experimental plate size. The primary paper’s extra third indexing round is assessed only to resolve the transposome label and is not added to the depicted route. The endpoint is a sequencing-ready library, with the readout explained from the primary paper.

states.label: Pooled indexed cDNA library ready for sequencing
features: The endpoint is DNA, not the original RNA. Multicolored linear library products are labelled Index 2, Index 1, UMI and cDNA.
The two rounds of cell indexing are RT-well and PCR-well identity. Illumina i5/i7 sequencing indexes are not, by themselves, evidence for additional split-pool rounds.
The primary Figure 1B assigns Index2/read1 to the i5 index, UMI and RT barcode, and Index1/read2 to the i7 index and cDNA fragment.

Sequencing these products yields preferential 3′ transcript tags: cDNA sequence supports gene/transcript-origin assignment; the paired cellular barcodes group tags by inferred cell/nucleus, and UMIs enable digital counting of captured molecules.
Barcode combinations can collide between cells. Captured tags support expression profiles, not a guarantee of one barcode combination per biological cell or complete full-length transcript recovery.

PolyT priming selects a polyadenylated-RNA representation but is not perfectly specific to mature mRNA: the paper notes possible priming at internal poly(dA) tracts in nuclear RNA. Sequencing and computational analysis are not separate operations depicted in this row.
